Technology in Thiel's sense is instead vertical: new ways of doing things that did not exist — the typewriter, the car, the computer, online payment. Note that technology here does not mean IT: a new business model, a new distribution or a new combination can be as vertical as a new chip design.

That is why new markets are almost always dominated by their creator for a long time, while open markets are dominated by whoever scales cheapest.

poster.text: The context first: 1999 was the year when everything seemed to work — venture capital flowed, business plans without revenue were listed, and thirty-year-olds became paper billionaires. The crash from 2000 to 2002 wiped out trillions in value, and the entrepreneurial world drew its conclusions. The four lessons became a new orthodoxy: make incremental improvements instead of radical new things; be lean and flexible and iterate instead of planning; improve what competitors already do instead of seeking new markets; and focus on the product instead of sales. Thiel's counterargument is empirical: the companies that built the following decade's greatest values did roughly the opposite on every point — they made bold leaps, planned, sought new markets and built distribution from day one.

poster.text: Thiel's deeper point is the symmetry: the nineties' mistake was believing that everything works; the two-thousands' mistake became believing that nothing works. The truth is that it is never as good or as bad as it looks — euphoria and panic are both bad advisers, because both replace the question is this real? with the question what does it feel like?. It is also the economics of a mood cycle: in euphoria, 1-to-n scalings (global copies) are priced as if they were 0-to-1 monopolies (created markets), and in panic, 0-to-1 monopolies are priced as if they were fads. Both errors are buying and selling opportunities for those who can tell the kind from the mood.

poster.text: For AK1A the chapter becomes a method rule in three steps. One — cleanse V01 for sentiment: growth forecasts written in euphoria's peak years should be discounted, and growth valuations at panic's bottom should be examined for cash-rich survivors rather than valued assets. Two — look for the overcorrected lesson: every crash leaves an orthodoxy that forbids something that actually works (after 2000: planning, niching, selling) — whoever identifies the prohibition can buy the forbidden cheaply. Three — be paranoid in the right way: paranoia is a bad planning tool but a good risk tool; do not ask how do I avoid being fooled again, but what is true regardless of mood — that is the question that drives both good companies and good analyses.

poster.text: The numbers Thiel puts on the table (2012): the American airline took on average 178 dollars per passenger trip and kept 37 cents in profit — the industry's entire history is essentially a long liquidation of capital through price wars and overcapacity. Google kept the same year roughly 21 cents of every revenue dollar in profit. The airline industry creates enormous value for the world and captures a negligible share of it; Google creates less value measured in saved hours but captures a valuation multiple of the airline industry's combined profits. The lesson is twofold: creating value is not the same as capturing value, and market structure — not product quality alone — determines the difference. A mediocre company in a monopoly structure beats an excellent company in a competitive structure, almost every time.

poster.text: Then the masquerade, the chapter's most important analytical contribution. Monopoly companies hide their position — Google likes to describe itself as an advertising company and can then say it has only a few percent of the global advertising market, when in search advertising — where the decisions are actually made — it controls around two thirds. The reframing hides the monopoly from antitrust authorities and from its own shame: in America's religion of competition it is ugly to be a monopoly. Conversely, weak companies hide their competition: the restaurant that calls itself the only British restaurant in Palo Alto does not have a niche — it has a location, and guests who can go anywhere. The translation for your analysis: a company's own market definition is always an interest-driven document; your task is to define the market by the buyer's actual substitutes, not by the seller's comfortable frames.

poster.text: And the psychology of competition, which Thiel describes as an ideology: school scores us on the same test, academia turns competing into a career, and business metaphors are military. Competition can drive performance — but it twists the focus from creating value to beating the opponent, and in a rat-race state the profit disappears to the customers. poster.text: Wall one: proprietary technology — and Thiel's rule of thumb is merciless: the product must be at least ten times better than the nearest alternative on something the customer cares about. Ten percent better is manageable for competitors and invisible to customers; ten times better changes behavior. Amazon's book selection at launch was an order of magnitude larger than every bookstore's; PayPal made online payments infinitely faster than checks. Note that the 10x test applies to what the customer actually values — a ten-times-better database the customer never notices is not a wall. Wall two: network effects — the product becomes more valuable per new user, and networks can only start small: Facebook began with Harvard students, not with the whole world. A network that ignites in a cohesive group is nearly impossible to attack from the outside.

The wall lies in the substance, not in the logo. Together the four give the construction method: start by monopolizing a small, concrete market (Amazon started with books; PayPal ignored everyone except the roughly twenty thousand so-called PowerSellers trading on eBay — a group small enough to dominate and clear enough to understand), and then scale upward in concentric circles: books became everything, eBay sellers became all online payments.

poster.text: The matrix. Definite optimism: America from the postwar era through the sixties, when engineers and planners drew highways, put people on the moon and built nuclear power plants with ten-year horizons — the future was assumed to be shapeable and was shaped. poster.text: The power law, in the Pareto tradition, means that a small minority of events accounts for the majority of the outcome — orders of magnitude that do not fit in the normal distribution's world. poster.text: What is a secret? Something true, important and not widely known — as opposed to the trivial (known to everyone) and the impossible (known to no one). Thiel's market test is the core of investing formulated as a founder's question: what valuable company is being built by nobody? poster.text: The scales of distribution, by price level. Complex sales: multimillion agreements are sold by the company's own top executives, face to face, over months (the space industry, large enterprise systems); one or two deals a year can carry an entire company. Personal sales: mid-class agreements that require a sales team but not a CEO — the engine of modern SaaS companies. The dead zone of distribution: products too cheap to justify salespeople but too expensive for pure advertising — here most small-business products die. Advertising and brand: consumer scale — large volumes, little interaction. Viral growth: the product carries its own distribution — PayPal's example is canonical: ten dollars in sign-up bonus and ten dollars to whoever recruited, an acquisition cost of roughly twenty dollars per customer, daily growth in the range of seven to ten percent during the expansion — the product spread because usage was its own reward. And every level has its rule: companies that master one channel win; companies that half-master several lose against both specialists.

poster.text: The twenty-first century's fear of substitution has twentieth-century predecessors: the Luddites, who smashed looms, and their intellectual heirs, who predicted that computerization would wipe out work. Thiel's answer is a distinction: computers are better than humans at processing enormous data sets by explicit rules; humans are better at formulating problems, understanding context and making judgment calls on incomplete information. Because the strengths are different, the exchange is not substitution but complementarity: the most valuable combination is the human who sets the goal and judges the outcome, the machine that scales the processing. Deep Blue's victory over Kasparov in 1997 proved the machine's power in a closed domain with known rules — not its ability to decide which questions are worth asking.

poster.text: The seven questions every company must answer — the course's checklist concentrate. One, engineering: is the product at least ten times better than the nearest substitute? Two, timing: why is this the right moment — what has changed? Three, monopoly: does the company start in a small market it can dominate? Four, people: does the team have the right competence — engineers for an engineering task, not salesmen with a story? Five, distribution: is there a thought-through path to the customer? Six, durability: will the position defend itself in ten to twenty years? Seven, secret: what does this company see that others do not? Tesla is the proof: engineering — an integrated electric car all the way down into the platform, not a combustion car with a battery; timing — the electric car's breakout coincided with the fall in battery cost and a state credit of 465 million dollars in 2010; monopoly — began in the small niche of luxury cars and owned it, before the descent toward the mass market; people — engineers with the product at the center; distribution — own stores without a dealer layer; durability — the head start and the pace; secret — that green was a status question: the car that made its owner cool, not ascetic. Answers to seven out of seven — and the company survived an industry that did not.

The stock market is the secondary market of that building process — and whoever understands 0-to-1 thinking knows where the next tail comes from.
